question.text: The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty began construction of this waterway, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic Ocean through its namesake country.
question.clue: The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty provided a strip of land twenty miles wide for this structure, whose construction was supervised by George Washington Goethals.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about odd presidential pets.
swap.text: This president owned a pet raccoon named Rebecca. This former Massachusetts governor famously said "You lose" to a woman who tried to win a bet by getting him to say more than two words.
swap.clue: This man won an election where he defeated the third-party Progressive candidate Robert La Follette as well as John W. Davis.

question.leadin: After this event, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris were tried for murder.
question.text: Name this event, in which the Asch building was set ablaze. During this event, many garment workers were unable to escape because the exterior doors were locked.
question.clue: It was the focus of twenty-three civil suits filed against Max Blanck and Issac Harris, who were acquitted of any wrongdoing, and it spurred the creation of a committee headed by Robert Wagoner, Al Smith, and Samuel Gompers.

swap.text: The bloodiest battle of the war took place on this Cuban hill, which was near Teddy Roosevelt's Rough Riders and the Buffalo Soldiers on Kettle Hill.
swap.clue: This battle was the land support for a naval operation led by William Sampson and Winfield Schley that drove Pascual Cervera from the nearby harbor.

question.leadin: Among the many cities visited by it were Honolulu, Sydney, and Yokohama.
question.text: Name this American Naval fleet that sailed around the world from 1907 through 1909. It was commissioned by Theodore Roosevelt.
question.clue: Initially the overall commander was Robley Evans, but he was replaced by Charles Sperry from the Fourth Division upon the first arrival at San Francisco.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Hull House, a settlement house that was a hub of social reform in the early 20th century.
swap.text: This American reformer founded Hull House with Ellen Starr as a "community of university women," who would teach classes to working-class people. She was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931.
swap.clue: This activist advocated for recreation as a way of addressing juvenile delinquency in her book The Spirit of Youth and the City Streets.

question.leadin: Name these members of U.S. organizations called the Progressive Party.
question.text: This Wisconsin senator ran for president in 1924 as a Progressive candidate and notably forced the U.S. not to join the League of Nations. Joseph McCarthy later became a senator by defeating this man's son.
question.clue: Before being a cabinet member, this person was the president of Ford Motors, and afterward, he was the president of the World Bank.

swap.leadin: He was represented by Clarence Darlow in court.
swap.text: Name this man who was imprisoned for some time in the 1900s and ran as a Socialist candidate in four different elections.
swap.clue: This man later helped found a political party on whose ticket he ran five times.

question.leadin: Hollywood mogul Cecil B. De Mille pledged a private army of 75 men and a machine gun to defend Los Angeles in the panic after this document was revealed.
question.text: Name this document revealed to the public on March 1, 1917 that promised one country certain "lost territory."
question.clue: It was first publicly used in an attempt to break a filibuster led by George Norris and Robert LaFollette.

swap.leadin: Name these "amendments" governing the Latin American policy of the U.S.
swap.text: This law, named for the Connecticut senator who put it forth on behalf of Secretary of State Root, permitted an exclusive U.S. right to intervene in Cuba.
swap.clue: This legislation prohibited a certain entity from entering into debt that it could not pay, or from making territorial concessions to anybody except the United States.

question.text: In this 1919 case, Chief Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes used the term "clear and present danger" with regards to first amendment speech rights.
question.clue: This Supreme Court case ruled that speech could be regulated if there was a "clear and present danger." Its Oliver Wendell Holmes-penned opinion popularized the expression "shouting fire in a crowded theater."

swap.leadin: Answer the following about American "muckraking" authors.
swap.text: Writer Edwin Markham helped expose this practice, which was restricted by the Keating-Owen Act, an act ruled unconstitutional in the case Hammer v. Dagenhart. This practice was protested in a 1903 march organized by Mother Jones.
swap.clue: The Reverend Alexander McKelway vocally advocated for a law regarding this practice that was later shot down in Hammer v. Dagenhart.

question.leadin: History has not looked fondly at some of the people Warren G. Harding appointed to his cabinet.
question.text: Harding may have mistakenly chosen this cabinet member, whose illegal leasing of federal lands was investigated by Thomas Walsh during the Teapot Dome Scandal.
question.clue: As a result, those two became the first two senators from his state, New Mexico, where he owned the massive Tularosa ranch at Three Rivers.

swap.leadin: This activist's mentor Johann Most is credited with popularizing the term "propaganda of the deed."
swap.text: Name this activist who wrote in the journal Mother Earth and was later deported with her partner, Alexander Berkman, on the Buford.
swap.clue: She was boycotted by the British left after discussing her horror with Leninism in My Disillusionment in Russia, and her other writings include the periodical Mother Earth.

question.text: Carrie Chapman Catt, the founder of this American organization, encouraged the Icelandic suffragette movement by enlisting Briet Bjarnheðinsdottir ("BREE-yet bjarn-HAY-theens-DOH-teer"). The NAWSA was succeeded by this organization that sponsored the U.S. presidential debates between 1976 and 1984.
question.clue: After winning the right to vote, NAWSA was reconstituted as this advocacy group. Prior to 1988, this group organized U.S. presidential debates.

swap.leadin: This company was accidentally sabotaged by "Joybubbles," a 7-year-old with perfect pitch; that feat was replicated by John Draper using Captain Crunch pirate whistles.
swap.text: Name this company that signed the Kingsbury Commitment to avoid one antitrust suit, but faced another in 1982. This company was purchased by its former subsidiary SBC in 2005.

question.leadin: Identify the following about the American home front during World War I.
question.text: These volunteers gave short patriotic speeches and sung nationalistic songs to drum up support for the war. They often gave their speeches in movie theaters and they received information from the Committee on Public Information.

swap.leadin: The editor of this newspaper managed to convince Mayor James M. Curley to shut down productions of The Clansman, but was unable to halt the premiere of Birth of a Nation at the Tremont Theatre a decade later.
swap.text: Name this militant Black newspaper that operated out of the former home of The Liberator. An editor of this newspaper was arrested after verbally sparring with Booker T. Washington during a chaotic 1903 speech.
swap.answerHtml: The Boston Guardian [accept The Guardian] (Washington’s 1903 speech to the Boston branch of the National Negro Business League devolved into the chaotic, but peaceful, “Boston Riot.”)

question.leadin: She was the first president of the Negro Fellowship League, which provided assistance to black migrants in the north, and her life's work was chronicled in A Red Record and Crusade for Justice.

swap.text: This Attorney General gave the Medicinal Alcohol Movement a meager win when his office chose not to limit the number of permits for physicians to prescribe wine and beer. This Attorney General set up the "Radical Division" but was opposed by Bureau of Immigration head Louis F. Post.
swap.clue: Acting Secretary of Labor Louis Post undid many of this man's actions, which included a crackdown on the Union of Russian Workers for producing an anarchist manifesto.
